beats.say: The Ottoman cannons thundered, but the real surprise was the hidden Byzantine spy network feeding false intel.
On May 29, 1453, a lone Greek engineer sabotaged a crucial gunpowder depot, delaying the final breach.

beats.say: Mehmed's elite Janissaries waited, unaware that a sudden storm turned the Golden Horn's waters into a treacherous swamp.
The famed chain across the harbor snapped when a massive cannonball hit its iron links, opening a secret escape route.
Inside Hagia Sophia, a hidden cellar housed priceless relics that the Ottomans ignored, fearing a cursed blast.
Meanwhile, a Venetian merchant smuggled a message to Genoa, warning of the empire's imminent fall days earlier.
The Byzantine defenders, low on morale, fought bravely until a sudden fire lit the city's western walls.
When the walls finally collapsed, the Ottoman flag rose, yet the city's libraries survived hidden beneath rubble.
Historians once claimed the cannons alone won the day, but secret sabotage proved decisive.
Thus, the fall of Constantinople was as much a story of shadows as of steel.
